extracted.intended_audience: researchers and scientists interested in research methodology and collaborative experimental design
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on conducting adversarial collaborations: a research method where opposing camps jointly design, run, and publish studies to resolve scientific disputes. Covers what it is, when it is feasible, benefits, and typical procedural elements (e.g., neutral moderation, co-design, transparency).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: opposing views collaborate
rubrics_metrics.description: In science, adversarial collaboration is a modality of collaboration wherein opposing views work together in order to jointly advance knowledge of the area under dispute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Can take the form of a scientific experiment conducted by two groups of experimenters with competing hypotheses, with the aim of constructing and implementing an experimental design in a way that satisfies both groups that there are no obvious biases or weaknesses in the experimental design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Co-designed experiment
rubrics_metrics.description: Adversarial collaboration can lead to a co-designed experiment and joint publishing of findings in order to resolve differences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parties jointly construct the experimental design so that both sides agree the design addresses key concerns and avoids obvious biases or weaknesses; this joint design is part of the route to resolving differing empirical claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Neutral moderator involvement
rubrics_metrics.description: Adversarial collaboration can involve a neutral moderator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A neutral third party may facilitate negotiations and experimental design to help ensure fairness and to broker agreements between antagonistic researchers (example: Edwin Locke acting as neutral party in Latham–Erez collaboration).

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency and open science
rubrics_metrics.description: With its emphasis on transparency throughout the research process, adversarial collaboration has been described as sitting within the open science framework.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transparency across design, analysis, and reporting is central; open-science practices help ensure that the collaboration and its findings are inspectable and reproducible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feasibility conditions — when collaboration is most feasible
rubrics_metrics.description: Adversarial collaboration is most feasible when least needed: when the clashing camps have advanced testable theories, subscribe to common canons for testing those theories, and disagreements are robust but respectful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ideal candidates are disputes where both sides have clearly articulated, testable hypotheses and accept common methodological standards, making joint experimental tests practicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infeasibility / anti-patterns — when collaboration is least feasible
rubrics_metrics.description: Adversarial collaboration is least feasible when most needed: when the scientific community lacks clear criteria for falsifying points of view, disagrees on key methodological issues, relies on second- or third-best substitute methods for testing causality, and is fractured into opposing camps that engage in ad hominem posturing and that have intimate ties to political actors who see any concession as weakness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not expect successful adversarial collaboration where parties cannot agree on falsification criteria, disagree fundamentally on methods, rely on weak substitutes for causal tests, or are hostile and politically entangled; these conditions undermine the possibility of a jointly accepted experimental test.

rubrics_metrics.name: Benefit — reduction of cognitive-motivational biases
rubrics_metrics.description: Adversarial collaboration has been recommended as a way of reducing the distorting impact of cognitive-motivational biases on human reasoning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: By forcing rivals to agree on design and tests, the process reduces bias-driven idiosyncratic choices about methods, analyses, and interpretation that can favor one side's prior beliefs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Benefit — resolving contentious or fringe science issues
rubrics_metrics.description: Adversarial collaboration has been recommended as a way of resolving contentious issues in fringe science.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using jointly agreed experimental designs can help adjudicate claims at the margins of accepted science by exposing which findings withstand jointly acceptable tests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application — improving academic commentaries
rubrics_metrics.description: Adversarial collaboration has been recommended as a potential solution for improving academic commentaries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structured adversarial collaborations can produce more constructive, evidence-focused commentaries by having opposing authors cooperate on empirical tests rather than merely trading critiques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose — improving science's self-correction
rubrics_metrics.description: Adversarial collaboration is proposed as a vehicle for improving how science can self-correct through exploring rival hypotheses which will ultimately expose false claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: By directly pitting rival hypotheses against jointly accepted tests, adversarial collaboration helps identify which claims fail under scrutiny and thereby accelerates correction of scientific errors.
